concepts.title: What aircraft construction covers
concepts.explain: Chapter 3 introduces how aircraft are designed and built, how their structures work, and how basic components and flight instruments support controlled flight. Detailed aerodynamics follows in later chapters.
concepts.apply: When studying a new airplane, identify the structure, controls, powerplant, landing gear, and displays before focusing on performance.

concepts.title: Certification starts with a design standard
concepts.explain: The FAA certifies aviation products—aircraft, engines, and propellers—against applicable airworthiness standards in Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations. Different products and categories have different standards.
concepts.apply: An airplane and a transport-category rotorcraft do not use one identical set of design requirements.

concepts.title: A type certificate applies to a product design
concepts.explain: When a design meets its applicable standards, the FAA can issue a type certificate. The Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS) records important approved design details and limitations.
concepts.apply: An aircraft model's approved engine or propeller configuration should agree with its certification documentation.

concepts.title: Production approval is a separate step
concepts.explain: Design approval does not itself mean a manufacturer may produce unlimited aircraft without oversight. Production approval addresses manufacturing controls and conformity to the approved design.
concepts.apply: A properly built replacement component must match the approved requirements, not simply look similar.

concepts.title: An airworthiness certificate is for an individual aircraft
concepts.explain: An individual aircraft must be eligible for an airworthiness certificate; its continuing condition and maintenance are separate from the original design's type certification.
concepts.apply: A certified model can still be unairworthy today because of damage, overdue inspection, or an unresolved defect.

concepts.title: Certification and maintenance are different responsibilities
concepts.explain: The initial approval establishes a design basis. The aircraft must then be maintained and operated in accordance with applicable limitations and rules.
concepts.apply: During preflight, the pilot cannot assume that a manufacturer's certified design guarantees that this particular airplane is ready to fly.

check.question: Which statement is most accurate?
options: Every aircraft of a certified model is automatically airworthy
A type certificate approves a design; an individual aircraft must still be airworthy
Production approval makes aircraft maintenance unnecessary
check.explanation: FAA design certification and the individual aircraft’s continuing airworthiness are distinct.

concepts.title: Thrust
concepts.explain: The propeller or other propulsion system creates thrust, a force that generally moves the aircraft forward. Thrust is not the same thing as lift.
concepts.apply: Increasing engine power can change the airplane's energy state, but a safe climb also requires managing attitude and airspeed.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-1 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Drag
concepts.explain: Drag is aerodynamic resistance to motion through the air. It opposes an aircraft's movement and changes with configuration and speed.
concepts.apply: Extending flaps or landing gear can increase drag, depending on design and configuration.

concepts.title: Weight
concepts.explain: Weight is the gravitational force acting on the airplane, including the aircraft, occupants, fuel, and baggage.
concepts.apply: Loading more baggage changes weight and may affect takeoff performance and handling.

concepts.title: Lift
concepts.explain: Lift is an aerodynamic force produced by airflow over lifting surfaces and is oriented perpendicular to the relative flight path. It generally counteracts weight in steady, level flight.
concepts.apply: A wing still produces aerodynamic forces during a descent; do not equate “descending” with “no lift.”

concepts.title: Forces change with the maneuver
concepts.explain: The familiar force diagram illustrates four forces, but their magnitudes need not be equal during acceleration, a climb, or a descent.
concepts.apply: A plane accelerating on takeoff is not in the same force balance as one flying straight and level at constant speed.

check.question: In straight, unaccelerated level flight, which force generally opposes weight?
options: Drag
Lift
Thrust
check.explanation: Lift acts generally upward in level flight and balances weight when vertical acceleration is zero.

concepts.title: Longitudinal axis: roll
concepts.explain: The longitudinal axis runs from nose to tail through the center of gravity. Rotation about it is roll: one wing rises while the other lowers.
concepts.apply: An aileron input banks the airplane by creating a rolling moment.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-2 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Lateral axis: pitch
concepts.explain: The lateral axis runs across the wings. Rotation about it is pitch: the nose rises or falls.
concepts.apply: The elevator is the primary pitch control on many airplanes.

concepts.title: Vertical axis: yaw
concepts.explain: The vertical axis runs vertically through the aircraft. Rotation about it moves the nose left or right relative to the flight path.
concepts.apply: Rudder input is used to control yaw, including adverse yaw when coordinating turns.

concepts.title: The center of gravity is the reference
concepts.explain: The three principal rotational axes intersect near the aircraft's center of gravity (CG), the point used to represent its weight distribution.
concepts.apply: If loading moves the CG, stability and control characteristics can change even though the pilot uses the same controls.

concepts.title: Motions can happen together
concepts.explain: During a coordinated maneuver, pitch, roll, and yaw can occur in combination; the axes are useful ways to understand each contribution.
concepts.apply: A properly coordinated turn involves bank and changes in heading; it is not merely turning the nose with rudder.

check.question: Which axis does an airplane rotate around when it rolls?
options: Vertical
Lateral
Longitudinal
check.explanation: Roll occurs about the nose-to-tail, longitudinal axis.

concepts.title: CG is the balance location
concepts.explain: The center of gravity is the point where the combined aircraft weight can be considered to act. Fuel, baggage, passengers, and equipment all influence it.
concepts.apply: Moving baggage aft may move the CG even if total weight remains unchanged.

concepts.title: Why an excessively forward CG matters
concepts.explain: A forward CG can increase the required tail-down force and may leave insufficient elevator authority to raise the nose for landing.
concepts.apply: An airplane can be under maximum gross weight yet outside its forward CG limit.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-3 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Why an excessively aft CG matters
concepts.explain: An aft CG can reduce stability and may leave insufficient nose-down elevator authority for stall recovery.
concepts.apply: A pilot should never treat an aft CG as a harmless way to improve cruise efficiency.

concepts.title: Both weight and balance matter
concepts.explain: Operating inside the allowable CG envelope matters as much as staying below the airplane's maximum permitted weight. The specific limits are aircraft-dependent.
concepts.apply: Check the aircraft's current weight-and-balance calculation using its approved data.

concepts.title: Weight can change during flight
concepts.explain: Fuel consumption can change both weight and CG; the effect depends on tank location and aircraft design.
concepts.apply: A legal CG at takeoff does not automatically guarantee the CG remains within limits throughout the planned flight.

check.question: An airplane is below maximum weight but has its CG beyond the aft limit. Is it acceptable?
options: Yes, weight is the only limit
No, the CG must also be in the approved envelope
Only if the flight is short
check.explanation: Weight and CG limits are independent requirements.

concepts.title: Fuselage
concepts.explain: The fuselage is the main body that houses crew, passengers, cargo, and equipment and joins other major components.
concepts.apply: Identify where the cabin, firewall, wing attachments, and tail assembly connect on your training airplane.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-4 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Wings
concepts.explain: Wings are the principal lifting surfaces of conventional airplanes. Their shape and structural design vary with the intended mission.
concepts.apply: A high-wing trainer and a low-wing cruiser share the same basic lift role but differ in arrangement.

concepts.title: Empennage
concepts.explain: The tail assembly generally includes stabilizing surfaces and movable flight controls that contribute to pitch and yaw control.
concepts.apply: Point out the horizontal stabilizer, vertical stabilizer, elevator, and rudder during a walkaround.

concepts.title: Powerplant
concepts.explain: On many small propeller airplanes, the powerplant includes the engine and propeller, supplying thrust and auxiliary power as equipped.
concepts.apply: Recognize the engine cowling, propeller, exhaust, air intakes, and applicable inspection items.

concepts.title: Landing gear
concepts.explain: Landing gear supports the aircraft while on the ground and during takeoff and landing. Configurations differ by mission and design.
concepts.apply: Know whether your aircraft uses a nosewheel or tailwheel and the normal ground-steering arrangement.

concepts.title: Monoplane and biplane
concepts.explain: A monoplane uses one principal wing plane, whereas a biplane uses two stacked wing planes. This describes wing arrangement, not necessarily speed or flight capability.
concepts.apply: Compare a familiar trainer with an early two-wing aircraft.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-6 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Spars carry major wing loads
concepts.explain: A spar is a principal structural member running spanwise, resisting significant wing loads.
concepts.apply: Do not confuse the thin visible skin with all the internal structure supporting the wing.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-7 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Ribs shape the airfoil
concepts.explain: Ribs help maintain the wing's cross-sectional shape and transfer loads to other structural members.
concepts.apply: A maintenance cutaway makes clear why wing construction is more than an outer shell.

concepts.title: Stringers and skin
concepts.explain: Stringers help stiffen the structure; wing skin creates the aerodynamic surface and can carry structural load in stressed-skin designs.
concepts.apply: Damage to a stressed panel can have implications beyond cosmetic appearance.

concepts.title: Ailerons control roll
concepts.explain: Ailerons normally move in opposite directions on the wings to create a rolling moment.
concepts.apply: When you move the yoke left, observe the ailerons and verify the correct response during preflight.

concepts.title: Flaps change wing characteristics
concepts.explain: Flaps generally extend together and change the wing's lift and drag characteristics for takeoff or landing. Their exact effect depends on design and setting.
concepts.apply: Use the aircraft's POH/AFM for permitted flap settings and performance changes rather than assuming all designs behave identically.

concepts.title: Wing design suits the mission
concepts.explain: Wing planform, arrangement, and structural choices reflect intended operation, balancing aerodynamic and practical tradeoffs.
concepts.apply: A heavy transport wing and a simple trainer wing are designed for different requirements.

title: Flap Designs and How They Differ

concepts.title: Plain flap
concepts.explain: A plain flap hinges downward from the trailing edge and changes wing curvature, increasing lift and drag depending on deflection.
concepts.apply: Identify the basic hinged motion in the FAA figure.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-8 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Split flap
concepts.explain: A split flap lowers from the bottom surface while the upper wing contour remains more continuous, typically producing considerable drag.
concepts.apply: Recognize why flaps are not simply interchangeable between airplane types.

concepts.title: Slotted flap
concepts.explain: A slot allows high-energy air to flow toward the upper surface, helping delay flow separation at higher flap deflections.
concepts.apply: The visible gap in a slotted flap has an aerodynamic purpose.

concepts.title: Fowler flap
concepts.explain: A Fowler flap moves aft as well as downward, increasing effective wing area and camber.
concepts.apply: Compare its travel with the simpler hinge action of a plain flap.

concepts.title: Slotted Fowler flap
concepts.explain: A design can combine aft travel with slots to achieve greater lift capability in a high-lift configuration.
concepts.apply: Notice the multi-part mechanism on some transport airplanes.

concepts.title: Flap settings must come from the airplane
concepts.explain: The handbook illustrates typical types, not universally safe deployment speeds or configurations.
concepts.apply: Always check the flap operating range and procedures in your airplane's POH/AFM.

check.question: Which flap moves rearward, increasing effective wing area as it deploys?
options: Fowler flap
Plain flap only
Split flap only
check.explanation: A Fowler flap travels aft as it deploys, unlike a simple hinged plain flap.

concepts.title: Not every aircraft uses conventional ailerons
concepts.explain: The handbook introduces different wing arrangements, including weight-shift-control aircraft that maneuver by changing the suspended mass position relative to the wing.
concepts.apply: Avoid assuming every winged aircraft has the same control inputs as a typical Cessna.

concepts.title: Wing shape follows intended use
concepts.explain: A wing's sweep, flexibility, and structural arrangement reflect the aircraft's aerodynamic and control requirements.
concepts.apply: Compare a flexible weight-shift wing with a rigid airplane wing.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-9 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Weight shift changes control moments
concepts.explain: On a weight-shift aircraft, the pilot changes the relative position of the carriage and wing to command changes in flight path and attitude.
concepts.apply: This is a different control mechanism, not just a different grip on an ordinary aileron system.

concepts.title: Use aircraft-category-specific references
concepts.explain: The Chapter 3 overview is not a complete operating manual for weight-shift aircraft.
concepts.apply: Follow the relevant FAA handbook and approved documentation for your aircraft category.

title: The Tail: Elevator, Rudder, and Trim

concepts.title: Vertical stabilizer
concepts.explain: The fixed vertical surface helps provide directional stability.
concepts.apply: Locate it before checking the attached rudder.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-10 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Rudder
concepts.explain: The rudder generally moves side-to-side on the vertical stabilizer to create yawing moments.
concepts.apply: Observe that rudder-pedal movement produces the expected deflection during the walkaround.

concepts.title: Horizontal stabilizer
concepts.explain: The horizontal tail surface helps provide longitudinal stability and supports pitch-control arrangements.
concepts.apply: Learn whether your aircraft uses a separate elevator or a movable stabilator.

concepts.title: Elevator
concepts.explain: The elevator pivots on a horizontal tail surface and changes aerodynamic forces to control pitch.
concepts.apply: A backward yoke movement usually commands a nose-up pitching moment.

concepts.title: Trim tabs
concepts.explain: Trim systems reduce the control force a pilot must maintain; small tabs or other mechanisms can change the neutral control force.
concepts.apply: Trim relieves pressure—it does not replace attention to airspeed or aircraft attitude.

concepts.title: Stabilator
concepts.explain: A stabilator combines horizontal stabilizer and elevator functions into a moving surface; some use an antiservo tab for appropriate control feel.
concepts.apply: Do not mistake the entire moving horizontal tail of a stabilator airplane for a conventional fixed stabilizer.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-11 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Antiservo tab
concepts.explain: The antiservo tab in a stabilator system moves to increase stick-force feedback and can also provide trim, depending on installation.
concepts.apply: Understand the correct control-system configuration for your specific model before flight.

check.question: A stabilator differs from a conventional elevator because…
options: the whole horizontal tail surface pivots
it can only move the nose downward
it is another name for the rudder
check.explanation: A stabilator is an all-moving horizontal surface used for pitch control.

concepts.title: Landing gear supports ground operations
concepts.explain: Landing gear supports aircraft weight while parking, taxiing, taking off, and landing, and absorbs landing loads as designed.
concepts.apply: Know the correct preflight inspection points for struts, tires, brakes, and attachments.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-12 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Tricycle landing gear
concepts.explain: A tricycle arrangement has main gear plus a nosewheel. Ground handling characteristics differ from tailwheel airplanes.
concepts.apply: Identify what can steer the nosewheel and what role differential braking plays.

concepts.title: Conventional or tailwheel gear
concepts.explain: Conventional gear has two main wheels and a wheel near the tail, giving a different ground-handling geometry.
concepts.apply: Tailwheel airplanes may need specialized training and endorsement before serving as PIC where required.

concepts.title: Floats and skis
concepts.explain: Airplanes can be equipped for water or snow operations; landing-surface compatibility shapes equipment and procedures.
concepts.apply: A floatplane's landing gear may be floats rather than tires—operating technique is not interchangeable.

concepts.title: Fixed versus retractable gear
concepts.explain: Some landing gear remains exposed; other designs retract gear for lower drag. Aircraft-specific procedures determine its operation.
concepts.apply: A retractable gear design requires correct checks and speed-limit awareness.

concepts.title: Engine converts fuel energy into useful power
concepts.explain: In a typical piston-engine airplane, the engine turns the propeller; actual installations differ by aircraft.
concepts.apply: Check engine and propeller operation using the aircraft's procedures.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-13 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Propeller blades create aerodynamic force
concepts.explain: Rotating propeller blades act as airfoils, producing a component of aerodynamic force along the thrust direction.
concepts.apply: Changing blade pitch can affect efficiency and engine load on equipped airplanes.

concepts.title: Blade twist
concepts.explain: A propeller blade is typically twisted along its span because blade sections move at different rotational speeds. This helps maintain useful aerodynamic angles.
concepts.apply: Notice how the blade geometry changes from hub to tip.

concepts.title: The cowling has functions beyond appearance
concepts.explain: Engine cowling streamlines airflow and helps guide cooling air through the engine compartment.
concepts.apply: Loose cowling fasteners or blocked cooling openings are meaningful inspection findings.

concepts.title: Powerplant may support other systems
concepts.explain: Depending on aircraft design, the engine installation may drive electrical generation and other accessories.
concepts.apply: Understand which electrical and instrument functions remain available during an engine or alternator problem.

concepts.title: Fuel and electrical systems are aircraft-specific
concepts.explain: Chapter 3 introduces their basic roles; system layouts, emergency procedures, and limitations depend on the particular model.
concepts.apply: Study the relevant POH before assuming a fuel selector or electrical bus works like another airplane's.

concepts.title: Truss-type structure
concepts.explain: A truss fuselage uses a framework of members arranged to handle structural loads; coverings may help with streamlining rather than carrying the primary loads.
concepts.apply: Early and specialty aircraft often show why a visible frame can be the main structure.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-5 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Monocoque construction
concepts.explain: In monocoque construction, the outer shell carries much of the structural load, supported by shaping components.
concepts.apply: A crack in stressed skin can matter because the skin is part of the structure.

concepts.title: Semimonocoque construction
concepts.explain: Semimonocoque construction combines stressed skin with stringers, formers, and bulkheads to distribute loads and improve strength.
concepts.apply: This is common in modern metal aircraft fuselages.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-14 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Bulkheads and formers
concepts.explain: These transverse members help define shape and carry or distribute loads.
concepts.apply: Locate the cabin and fuselage sections where substantial structure supports attachments.

concepts.title: Stringers and longerons
concepts.explain: Longitudinal stiffeners improve the strength and stability of thin skin panels.
concepts.apply: The FAA figure clarifies why skin and internal framing work as a system.

concepts.title: Firewall
concepts.explain: A fire-resistant bulkhead separates the engine compartment from the cabin or cockpit in typical single-engine designs.
concepts.apply: Inspect the firewall region for signs of damage or unauthorized openings during appropriate maintenance checks.

check.question: What defines semimonocoque construction?
options: Only fabric stretched over a wing
Stressed skin reinforced by an internal framework
No structural skin at all
check.explanation: Semimonocoque combines load-carrying skin with internal reinforcement such as stringers and bulkheads.

concepts.title: A composite combines materials
concepts.explain: A structural composite typically combines reinforcing fibers with a matrix material, allowing designers to tailor properties in different directions.
concepts.apply: Composite construction is not the same as making an entire airplane from a single homogeneous plastic.

concepts.title: Fiberglass and carbon fiber
concepts.explain: Fiberglass and carbon fiber are examples of reinforcing materials used in aircraft composites, with differing strength, weight, and conductivity properties.
concepts.apply: Recognize that external appearance alone may not reveal the exact reinforcement used.

concepts.title: The role of the matrix
concepts.explain: Resin or another matrix holds fibers together and transfers loads between them. Construction technique and curing quality matter.
concepts.apply: Structural integrity depends on the system, not merely which fabric was selected.

concepts.title: Strength-to-weight benefit
concepts.explain: Properly designed composites can provide high strength with relatively low mass and allow complex aerodynamic shapes.
concepts.apply: More efficient structural weight can support the aircraft's performance goals.

concepts.title: Reduced corrosion potential
concepts.explain: Composites avoid some metal-corrosion mechanisms but introduce different inspection, maintenance, and environmental considerations.
concepts.apply: Never interpret “corrosion resistant” as “maintenance free.”

concepts.title: Composite construction has a long history
concepts.explain: The handbook traces aerospace composite use from earlier fiberglass developments to modern general aviation, helicopters, and transport airplanes.
concepts.apply: Comparing different aircraft demonstrates that composite materials are not limited to experimental aircraft.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-15 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Hidden damage is a central concern
concepts.explain: A composite part can sustain internal delamination or fiber damage even when external marks seem minor.
concepts.apply: After a strike or impact, do not dismiss a small dent based only on visible appearance.

concepts.title: Impact energy changes the damage pattern
concepts.explain: The handbook's diagrams show how different impact energies can produce different internal fracture patterns and externally visible clues.
concepts.apply: Damage depth and area may differ from what a quick surface check suggests.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-16 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Delamination weakens the load path
concepts.explain: Layers can separate internally; this can significantly alter a component's capacity to carry designed loads.
concepts.apply: Special inspection methods may be needed after an impact.

concepts.title: Not all composites conduct electricity like metal
concepts.explain: Fiberglass is an electrical insulator; carbon fiber conducts but not in the same way as aluminum. Aircraft may need conductive mesh for lightning protection.
concepts.apply: Repairs can involve restoring lightning protection as well as structural strength.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-17 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Temperature and moisture may matter
concepts.explain: Composite properties and repair processes depend on their materials and manufacturing methods.
concepts.apply: Approved repair instructions govern materials, preparation, layup, and curing.

concepts.title: Repairs require appropriate methods
concepts.explain: Composite damage cannot simply be treated like a cosmetic scratch or repaired using unapproved filler.
concepts.apply: Follow type-specific maintenance data and qualified personnel decisions.

check.question: A composite wing is struck, but only a small surface mark is visible. What is the concern?
options: Internal damage may extend beyond what is visible
Composites cannot be damaged by impacts
No inspection could ever detect a problem
check.explanation: Composite structures can sustain subsurface damage or delamination despite a small visible mark.

concepts.title: Analog instrument presentation
concepts.explain: Conventional instrument panels use individual gauges to display flight and engine information. They may rely on different sources and systems.
concepts.apply: Recognize the purpose of each instrument rather than memorizing its location alone.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-18 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Digital glass cockpit
concepts.explain: Electronic displays integrate flight, engine, and navigation data into configurable presentations; a single display can combine multiple functions.
concepts.apply: The same underlying flight parameter may appear as a tape, number, map, or symbolic representation.

concepts.title: Three functional groups
concepts.explain: Chapter 3 organizes the displayed information into performance, control, and navigation instruments; an aircraft may integrate information from several groups on one screen.
concepts.apply: Ask what information you need rather than assuming a glass cockpit means a different flying goal.

concepts.title: Cross-check is still required
concepts.explain: Regardless of display type, instruments can fail, be misread, or provide unexpected information. A disciplined scan connects indications with aircraft behavior.
concepts.apply: Compare attitude, performance, and external references as conditions permit.

concepts.title: The installed system matters
concepts.explain: The chapter compares examples but does not define every avionics suite. Specific controls, limitations, and abnormal procedures are aircraft dependent.
concepts.apply: Study the aircraft and avionics flight manuals before relying on any advanced display.

check.question: Which statement about a glass cockpit is best?
options: It changes the laws of flight
It integrates and presents information electronically
It eliminates the need for instrument interpretation
check.explanation: Digital displays change presentation and integration, not the physics or need for pilot interpretation.

title: Performance Instruments: What the Airplane Is Doing

concepts.title: Airspeed
concepts.explain: An airspeed indication provides speed-related information needed for aircraft control and operating limits.
concepts.apply: Respect the airplane's applicable speeds and instrument limitations in the POH/AFM.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-19 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Altitude
concepts.explain: The altimeter indicates altitude based on pressure measurements and proper setting; pilots must interpret it in context.
concepts.apply: An incorrect altimeter setting can lead to an incorrect altitude indication.

concepts.title: Vertical speed
concepts.explain: The vertical speed indicator reports rate of climb or descent, subject to instrument response characteristics.
concepts.apply: A stable indicated descent rate can help with approach energy management.

concepts.title: Heading and turn performance
concepts.explain: Heading and turn-related indications help show where the airplane is pointed and how its direction changes.
concepts.apply: Cross-check the relevant indications with the intended flight path.

concepts.title: Performance trends
concepts.explain: Digital and analog displays can show trends as well as instantaneous values; a trend cue is not a guarantee of what happens next.
concepts.apply: In rapidly changing conditions, remain ahead of the indications instead of chasing them.

concepts.title: Recognize grouped displays
concepts.explain: The FAA performance-instrument figure highlights where similar indications appear on traditional panels and electronic flight displays.
concepts.apply: Identify corresponding information on your specific trainer.

concepts.title: Attitude indicator
concepts.explain: The attitude indicator displays aircraft pitch and bank attitude relative to a reference, directly supporting precise control.
concepts.apply: An indicated nose-up attitude does not by itself tell you the airplane is climbing.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-20 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Power instruments
concepts.explain: Engine tachometer and manifold-pressure displays, where installed, tell the pilot how the engine is being commanded or performing.
concepts.apply: Selecting a familiar power setting helps create repeatable flight configurations.

concepts.title: Control versus performance
concepts.explain: Control instruments help show the immediate control inputs and attitude/power configuration; performance instruments show the resulting speed, altitude, or vertical-speed response.
concepts.apply: Set attitude and power, then cross-check whether the desired performance develops.

concepts.title: Small adjustments
concepts.explain: Precise flying often requires measured changes followed by time for the aircraft and instruments to settle.
concepts.apply: Avoid making a series of large pitch corrections before checking how airspeed and vertical speed respond.

concepts.title: Analog and glass representations
concepts.explain: A digital display can place pitch, bank, engine, and status data on different screens or within one integrated presentation.
concepts.apply: Learn where to find the same essential parameters if a display changes modes.

check.question: A pilot raises the nose and immediately sees pitch change. Which other information confirms the aircraft’s actual climb or descent?
options: Performance indications such as vertical speed and altitude trend
Only the radio frequency
Only the heading bug
check.explanation: Attitude is a control indication; performance is checked through altitude, vertical speed, and related indications.

concepts.title: Navigation instruments answer where to go
concepts.explain: Navigation information shows the aircraft's relationship to a route, a selected station, a fix, or a desired course.
concepts.apply: A correct heading alone does not guarantee tracking a desired course in wind.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-21 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Course deviation
concepts.explain: Course deviation indicators show whether the aircraft is left or right of a selected navigation course, with meaning that depends on the system.
concepts.apply: Interpret the instrument as a guidance cue rather than a direct rudder command.

concepts.title: VOR and other ground-based sources
concepts.explain: Traditional systems present bearing or course relationships to ground-based radio facilities; pilots need to know their operating principles and limitations.
concepts.apply: A navigation receiver indication must be interpreted with the proper frequency, course, and validity checks.

concepts.title: GPS and integrated navigation
concepts.explain: Satellite-based navigation systems can provide route and position information, often integrated into a moving map or primary display.
concepts.apply: Verify the active waypoint and course rather than following an old flight plan blindly.

concepts.title: Glideslope information
concepts.explain: Appropriate approach equipment can present vertical guidance relative to an approach path; the FAA example compares analog and digital depictions.
concepts.apply: Glideslope position has a specific meaning and must be interpreted with the relevant approach procedure.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook · Figure 3-22 — cropped from the original handbook

concepts.title: Navigation data must be verified
concepts.explain: An appealing display does not replace selection, monitoring, or cross-check of the actual navigation source and flight plan.
concepts.apply: Confirm the correct CDI source after changing navigation modes.

check.question: What does a course deviation indicator primarily help you assess?
options: Fuel quantity
Position relative to a selected navigation course
Engine oil temperature
check.explanation: CDI information reflects the aircraft’s relationship to selected course guidance.
